newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - June 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - June 13.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents.
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- PACIFICORP SEEKING 4.5 BILLION STG FOR ENERGY BID

Pacificorp, the US-based coal and electricity generator, is seeking a financing package in the region of $8 billion to $10 billion (4.5 billion stg to 6 billion stg) to complete its planned offer for The Energy Group, the demerged Hanson business. Pacificorp plans to fund the deal in part by selling assets worth $1.5 billion and providing $500,000 in cash, with the most likely candidate for disposal being its Pacific Telecom subsidiary.
-- BOOTS CHIEF IN 1 MILLION STG SHARE SALE TO FUND NEW OPTIONS

Boots has revealed that its chief executive, Lord Blyth, has sold shares in the group worth more than 1 million stg. The sale, completed Wednesday, is said to have been to allow Lord Blyth to finance the purchase of new options. Blyth must exercise his options on 190,000 shares by the end of the year under the group's new long-term incentive plan. Shares in Boots fell sharply on news of the sale, but recovered to close on Thursday up .5p at 735.5p.
-- GUINNESS MERGER SET FOR ARBITRATION

French luxury goods and spirits group LVMH is expected Friday to step up its campaign to halt the proposed merger between Grand Metropolitan and Guinness. LVMH is likely to apply for arbitration proceedings which, if successful, would force the group and Guinness to each appoint an arbitrator and to jointly appoint a third independent arbitrator. The process, which could take some months, would delay progress in the proposed merger.
THE TIMES
-- TOP THREE FORECAST TO FAIL EMU TEST

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) has predicted that France, German and Italy -- the three largest prospective members of an on-schedule single European currency -- would all fail to meet the Maastricht criteria. In its latest Economic Outlook, the OECD claims the three countries will all run budget deficits of 3.2 percent this year, higher than the Maastricht qualification criteria of 3 percent.
-- POWER MARKET TO START ON SCHEDULE

John Battle, the energy minister, has said that competition in the electricity sector will begin on time, but that consumers cannot expect any significant price reductions in the immediate future. Battle held a summit on Thursday with the heads of the regional electricity companies and with the industry regulator, Professor Stephen Littlechild. The meeting was dominated by discussions over the problems of introducing competition, due on April 1, 1998.
-- THREAT TO UK JOBS IN ELECTROLUX SHAKE-UP

Electrolux, the household appliances manufacturer, has announced that it is to cut 12,000 jobs worldwide, including the closure of 25 of its 150 plants. Although the Swedish company has yet to decide exactly where the cuts will fall, there are fears for thousands of British jobs. The cuts and closures, part of a massive restructuring programme, will take place over two years and are expected to cost some SKr2.5 billion (197 million stg).
THE GUARDIAN
-- WATCHDOG UNHOOKS BT SCHOOLS INTERNET PLAN

Oftel, the regulator of the UK telecommunications industry, has pulled the plug on plans by British Telecom to provide schools and libraries with cheap access to the Internet. The regulator is concerned that the proposal unduly favours BT's own Internet service as the company was insisting that access would only be provided to Internet service providers (ISP) which used its network. Most ISPs currently use the networks of BT rivals Mercury, Energis or cable companies.
-- EC POUNCES AFTER AMINO ACID PRICE-FIXING CLAIMS

Anti-trust investigators from the European Commission have raided the offices in Germany and Britain of two companies alleged to have been involved in price-fixing of lysine, an amino acid used in animal feed. The raids, at Archer-Daniels-Midland and Kyowa Hakko Kogyo, follow a price-fixing inquiry in the US involving the two companies and other Japanese and South Korean firms.
-- BLAIR MEETS LIKE MINDS AT FORD

Prime minister Tony Blair has held an hour-long meeting with directors of the Ford Motor Company. The move, which continues the new government's charm offensive with industry, was held at the vehicle maker's request, and coincided with the announcement of a 40 million stg investment at its instrument plant in north London. Following the meeting, Ford chairman and chief executive Alex Trotman said there had been "a meeting of minds and objectives on the economy", but he also warned against excessive European Union regulation and stressed the need for labour market flexibility.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- LABOUR URGED TO SET FIRM EMU TIMETABLE

Niall Fitzgerald, the chairman of Unilever and a leading advocate of British membership of a single European currency, has called for monetary union to be phased in, with countries joining as soon as they could achieve enough economic convergence. In a speech at the London School of Economics, Fitzgerald said that a delay to the project would be preferable to an on-schedule fudge, but he also urged the government to commit Britain to joining later on a firm timetable.
-- RETAIL SALES IN US FALL UNEXPECTEDLY

Statistics released in the US show that retail sales in the country fell an unexpected 0.1 percent in May, with the figure for April also being revised downward to a 0.9 percent decline. The negative retail sales figures prompted one analyst to suggest they represent "a very significant slowdown in consumer spending in the second quarter" which "contrasts very strongly with a very robust first quarter".
-- BT MAY TAKE CHARGES DISPUTE TO MMC

British Telecom has said that while it welcomes plans from industry regulator Oftel to bring all network charges into one framework with an overall price cap, the company has "major concerns" over the level of the proposed charges. BT has threatened to refer the issue to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission after Oftel proposed that the interconnection charges -- the amount BT charges rivals for access to its network -- should be cut by 10-20 percent from October and subject to a price cap of RPI minus 6-12 percent for the following three years.
